items.prompt: All tests pass. What does that confirm?
choices: Output is right for the inputs tested
The next change will be cheap to make
The structure of the code is clean
items.explanation: Tests check outputs for the cases they cover. They say nothing about how costly future changes are.

items.prompt: Which question measures design quality?
choices: Does it print the right answer?
What will the next change cost?
items.explanation: Design quality is about the cost of change, not about today's output.

items.prompt: Why is the cost of poor design easy to miss?
choices: It makes the program crash at once
It shows up later, on every change
items.explanation: Poor design works today. The bill arrives gradually, on later changes.

items.prompt: A month-1 change took 2 hours; a same-size change in month 6 took 3 weeks. What changed?
items.explanation: The request and the tests were the same. The accumulated structure made the change harder.

items.prompt: Who usually pays for poor design?
choices: Only the author on day one
items.explanation: The cost is deferred and lands on later changes, often on a different person.

items.prompt: Correctness answers which question?
choices: How easy is it to change?
items.explanation: Correctness is about right outputs. Ease of change is design quality.

items.prompt: Can code be correct and badly designed at once?
items.explanation: Passing tests and being costly to change are independent properties.

items.prompt: Design quality is mostly built from which two properties?
items.explanation: Coupling and cohesion drive how costly each change is.

items.prompt: A team says: "Every test has been green for six months, so our design must be healthy." What is wrong with that reasoning?
choices: Green tests show outputs are right, not what a change costs
Six months is too short a period to trust any green result
Green tests prove the design is healthy only for small projects
The tests are probably written against the wrong inputs
items.explanation: Tests measure correctness. Change cost is a separate property they never observe.
items.reference:
Two different questions
correctness: is the output right today?
design quality: what does the next change cost?
tests answer the first, not the second
Why: green tests say nothing about how expensive the next change will be.
items.learnMore:
Correctness is not design quality

A suite checks outputs for the inputs it covers. The cost of the next change depends on how the code is structured, which no output check sees.

Common mistake

Reading green tests as proof that the code is easy to change.
items.reflection: Think of something you built that worked perfectly but was painful to alter later. What would have told you early that it would be?

items.prompt: Two modules give identical outputs on every test. One takes ten times longer to extend. Which statement is true?
choices: The slower one must contain a bug that the tests missed
They are equally correct but differ in design quality
The faster one must have more test coverage overall than the slower
They are the same design, since the outputs match
items.explanation: Identical outputs mean equal correctness. The extension cost difference is design quality.

items.prompt: What does coupling describe?
choices: How many lines a function has
items.explanation: Coupling is the degree to which one piece depends on another.

items.prompt: With high coupling, changing module A tends to force...
items.explanation: That is the definition of entanglement: a change in one forces a change in the other.

items.prompt: Which is lower coupling?
choices: Copying another module's code into yours
Calling notify() on a stable interface
items.explanation: A narrow interface limits what can break.

items.prompt: A narrow, stable interface makes the breakage surface...
items.explanation: Fewer details to depend on means fewer ways to be broken.

items.prompt: Team A uses the mailer's internals; Team B calls notify(). Which is more tightly coupled?
items.explanation: Team A depends on implementation details that may change.

items.prompt: Does high coupling make today's tests fail?
choices: No, it raises the cost of later changes
items.explanation: Coupling is a cost on change, not a present-day failure.

items.prompt: Where should coupling be examined?
items.explanation: Hidden relationships behind an interface count too.

items.prompt: What should dependents rely on?
items.explanation: Depending on a promise, not on internals, keeps the surface small.

items.prompt: Team C's order code calls only notify(order), but the class behind notify() calls into three unrelated internal services directly. What is the accurate assessment?
choices: Low coupling at one boundary, high inside the notifier
Low coupling overall, since the order code is unaffected
High coupling overall, because the order code uses notify()
Coupling cannot be judged without seeing the tests
items.explanation: Coupling belongs to every relationship. The notifier's reach into three services is the same problem one layer deeper.
items.reference:
Coupling = breakage surface
high: depends on another piece's internals
low: depends on a small, stable interface
measure every relationship, not just one boundary
Why: the narrower the promise you depend on, the fewer outside changes can break you.
items.learnMore:
Coupling

Coupling is how much one piece depends on the details of another. Reaching into internals makes almost any change over there a possible break over here.

Common mistake

Checking one boundary and declaring the system loosely coupled while the pieces behind it still reach into each other.
items.reflection: Where in your daily life do you rely on a stable promise rather than on how something works inside? What would break if the inside changed?

items.prompt: The mailer's internal connection object is replaced. Team A's order code reaches into it; Team B's calls notify(). What happens?
choices: Both break, because both depend on the mailer in some way or other
Team A's code may break; Team B's survives if notify() keeps its meaning
Neither breaks, since the order code itself never changes at all
Team B's code breaks, because interfaces are more fragile
items.explanation: Only code that depends on the replaced internals breaks. The interface insulates Team B.

items.prompt: What does cohesion describe?
choices: Whether a module's jobs fit together
How long it takes to run
items.explanation: Cohesion is about how well a module's responsibilities fit together.

items.prompt: Low cohesion means a module has...
items.explanation: Unrelated responsibilities mean unrelated reasons for edits.

items.prompt: One class does pricing, email and analytics. Its cohesion is...
items.explanation: Three independent jobs in one place is low cohesion.

items.prompt: What is the test for cohesion?
choices: Do they touch the same data?
Are they in the same folder?
items.explanation: Shared reasons to change, not shared data or location.

items.prompt: Why does splitting by reason to change help?
choices: Edits for one reason risk fewer others
items.explanation: Smaller blast radius per edit.

items.prompt: Which has one reason to change?
choices: A class that prices and sends email
A file of random unrelated helpers
A class that only calculates prices
items.explanation: A single responsibility has a single reason to change.

items.prompt: Is high cohesion generally good or bad?
items.explanation: It keeps each change small and local.

items.prompt: Two methods both read the same order. Are they automatically cohesive?
items.explanation: Sharing data does not mean sharing a reason to change.

items.prompt: A developer splits one class into three, but each new class reaches into the other two to share state. What is the effect?
choices: Cohesion rose in each class, but coupling returned between them
Nothing changed, since the same code still exists in total
Cohesion and coupling both improved at once in the new design
Coupling fell, but cohesion inside each class fell too, in the end
items.explanation: The split gives single reasons to change, but reaching across classes re-creates entanglement.
items.reference:
Cohesion = one reason to change
low: pricing + email + analytics in one class
high: each class has a single reason to change
touching the same data is not enough
Why: pieces that change together belong together; pieces that don't, don't.
items.learnMore:
Cohesion

Ask of any two parts: would they ever change for the same reason? If not, bundling them means an edit for one risks the other.

Common mistake

Judging cohesion by shared data, or by file count, instead of by reasons to change.
items.reflection: Think of a drawer or folder that mixes unrelated things. What single question would you use to decide what belongs together?

items.prompt: Pricing code is split across six files that all change together whenever a tax rule changes. How cohesive is that design?
choices: Excellent: six small files are always more cohesive
Poor: the pieces share one reason to change yet live apart
Poor: six files is simply far too many for one single module
Excellent: each file now has fewer lines than before
items.explanation: Pieces that change together should sit together. File count is not the metric.

items.prompt: In the coupled design, each new channel costs...
items.explanation: Each lands in code more tangled than before.

items.prompt: In the decoupled design, adding a channel edits the order code...
items.explanation: A new notifier attaches to the list instead.

items.prompt: A 0% coupling penalty means each channel costs...
items.explanation: No growth per change gives a flat cost.

items.prompt: Model: 2 hours per channel, no penalty, 4 channels. Total?
Why does the coupled cost line curve upward?
items.explanation: More existing branches mean more to reason about per change.

items.prompt: At 4 channels, the gap between the two designs is...
items.explanation: About 8 versus 9.99 hours in the model.

items.prompt: In the decoupled design, where does the SMS-eligibility rule live?
items.explanation: It is text-message policy, so it belongs in the text notifier.

items.prompt: Compounding means growth applies to...
items.explanation: Each step multiplies the previous, grown value.

items.prompt: Model: 2 hours for the first channel, each later one 15% costlier. About how many total hours for 10 channels?
items.explanation: Summing 2, 2.3, 2.65, ... gives 40.61. Twenty is the no-penalty total; 85 comes from a 30% penalty.
items.reference:
Same start, different curve (model: 2h first change)
10 channels, no penalty: 20 hours
10 channels, 15% penalty: 40.61 hours
20 channels, 15% penalty: 204.89 hours (5.1x)
Why: a small per-change penalty compounds, because each change grows on the one before.
items.learnMore:
Compounding change cost

If every change costs a fixed percentage more than the last, the total grows faster than linearly. Early on the gap is small; later it dominates.

Common mistake

Judging the penalty by the first few changes, where the two curves look nearly identical.
items.reflection: Where have you seen small extra costs per step add up to something large over time, in money, effort or time?

items.prompt: A teammate says the 4-channel gap is only about 2 hours, so decoupling is not worth it. Best response?
choices: Agree, because a 2-hour gap proves compounding never matters in practice
The gap compounds: about 165 extra hours at 20 channels in the model
Disagree, because the gap at 4 channels is really about 20 hours
Agree, because channel count never rises past four
items.explanation: Judging by the early gap misses compounding: 204.89 minus 40 is about 165 hours at 20 channels.

items.explanation: Interactions grow with existing branches, so review and tests grow faster than the branch itself.

items.prompt: Technical debt is most like...
choices: A bug that was already fixed
items.explanation: A shortcut costs a little extra on every change built on it.

items.prompt: Over-engineering means...
choices: Building for needs not yet real
items.explanation: Abstractions for hypothetical needs are pure cost.

items.prompt: A module has not changed in two years and nothing is planned. Refactor?
items.explanation: The benefit needs a change to arrive.

items.prompt: Is a shortcut taken for a real deadline always wrong?
choices: No, a fair trade if repaid
items.explanation: Deliberate debt with a repayment plan can be reasonable.

items.prompt: Does splitting into more files mean more cohesion?
items.explanation: Cohesion is about independent reasons to change.

items.prompt: When does decoupling pay off?
items.explanation: The saving appears on later changes.

items.prompt: A refactor with no driving change risks...
items.explanation: Any rewrite can introduce bugs.

items.prompt: Only one notification channel will ever exist. Build the notifier list?
items.explanation: Without a second channel the abstraction never pays back.

items.prompt: A prototype will be thrown away in two weeks, and its code is tangled. What is the sound advice?
choices: Leave it: no later changes means no cost to repay
Rewrite it fully, since tangled code is never acceptable
Add abstractions now in case it is kept after all
Split it into many files to improve its cohesion
items.explanation: With no future changes, the interest is never charged, so cleanup is pure cost.
items.reference:
Invest where change is likely
real second requirement: decoupling pays
code untouched for years: leave it
deliberate shortcut: fine if repaid
Why: design work is a bet on future change, so size the bet to the change you expect.
items.learnMore:
Matching design to expected change

The saving from good design appears only when a change arrives. Frequently and unpredictably changing code earns more design; stable code earns less.

Common mistake

Treating all debt as bad, or all refactoring as good, instead of asking what change is driving it.
items.reflection: Think of something you maintain. Which part is likely to keep changing, and which could safely stay as it is?

items.prompt: Why is repaying debt left for two years costlier than repaying it at the second channel?
choices: Developers forget how the language works after two years
More code now sits on top of it and must change too
Old code is always slower to compile than new code
Refactors are billed per year of age by the framework
items.explanation: Each later change built on the shortcut adds more to untangle.
